newsitem.title: USA: Senate ends filibuster, passes aviation bill.
newsitem.headline: Senate ends filibuster, passes aviation bill.

text.p: The Senate voted on Thursday to cut off a filibuster mounted by pro-labour senators in an attempt to kill legislation they said would hamper efforts of Federal Express Corp truck drivers to join a union.

The vote was 66-31, six more than the majority needed to cut off debate. It cleared the way for enactment by a 92-2 vote of a bill providing billions of dollars for the Federal Aviation Administration and airport safety and anti-terrorism equipment.
Sen. Edward Kennedy, D-Mass., had led the drive to remove the FedEx provision from the bill, delaying Senate adjournment for the year.

The provision would have ensured that FedEx employees were covered by the Railway Labour Act, requiring the firm's truck drivers to organise nationally to join a union, rather than by the National Labour Relations Act, which allows more easily attainable local bargaining units.
The railway law covers airline pilots and FedEx's pilots are unionized. The truck drivers are not.

Supporters of the provision said it merely corrected a drafting error made when Congress enacted earlier legislation. Kennedy said it was a "union-busting" provision aimed at "stacking the deck" in pending litigation on the union issue.
Republican Leader Trent Lott warned the Senate that a bill containing funds for vital airport safety and terrorism equipment was being held up.
"I'm thinking about the families of (air crash) victims who have got to be horrified at what we've been doing in last few days," Lott said.
Both labour and FedEx, two big political campaign contributors, had lobbied heavily on the bill.

Although Kennedy repeatedly blasted Republicans for pushing the FedEx provision, it was actually attached to the bill by South Carolina Democrat Fritz Hollings when it was before a Senate-House conference committee.

Among the 31 senators voting against the motion to end the filibuster were Republican Sens Arlen Spector and Rick Santorum. The two are from Pennsylvania where FedEx truck drivers have been seeking to organise for several years.

The bill, which now goes to the White House, included anti- terrorism requirements that airlines do background checks on employees screening passengers, baggage and cargo and that the FAA certify security firms doing the screening.

The bill also established rules for record-setting flights stemming from the crash of a plane this year in which 7-year-old Jessica Dubroff was killed while trying to become the youngest pilot to fly across the country.
The rules would bar anyone without a valid pilot's certificate and medical certificate from handling the controls of a plane while trying to set a record.

Also in the measure were reforms of the way airlines deal with families of crash victims. They were taken from a separate bill drafted after complaints by families of victims of the July 17 TWA 800 crash off Long Island, New York.
